summary:
India's Parliament passed the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill in March 2026, replacing the 2019 law's self-identification route with legal recognition limited to historically accepted socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner, and to intersex individuals. Trans men, trans women and non-binary people who self-identify outside those categories fall outside the recognition scheme. Rights activists, among them Akkai Padmashali, describe the amendment as criminalising and an attack on the right to exist. The government presents it as widening access to welfare schemes and protection from trafficking; critics say it excludes many trans, non-binary and gender-fluid people. India has an estimated two million transgender people.

The baseline for entry and stay is mixed. Same-sex acts were decriminalised by the Supreme Court in 2018, and discrimination is barred on grounds including sex, which courts have interpreted to cover gender identity; the Supreme Court has held that discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity falls within Article 15's prohibition of discrimination by sex, and the Allahabad High Court extended that in 2021 to bar employment discrimination on sexual orientation grounds. There is no same-sex marriage or civil partnership, although courts have acknowledged same-sex couples as family units.

Criminal-law protection weakened in 2024. Replacing the Indian Penal Code with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita removed legal safeguards that had protected trans persons from sexual violence, and trans people fear a rise in assaults because the new code omits the gender-identity-specific offences the old law carried.

Identity documents and checkpoints are a live source of friction. In February 2026 the Allahabad High Court granted relief to a trans person who had been asked to take a medical exam by passport authorities. In November 2024 an openly transgender law student, Sakshi Jain, was stopped at Chennai International Airport Terminal 1 by Central Industrial Security Force personnel despite presenting her PAN card for identity verification. In Kolkata a transwoman alleged that a Railway Protection Force constable groped her at the station under the pretext of checking her gender, and transgender persons arrested by the Railway Protection Force in Assam have recounted degrading treatment in custody.

Assessments of police conduct diverge. The United Kingdom's December 2025 country policy note records limited reports of police abuse of LGBT+ people, likelier in conservative rural areas and not systemic; victim interviews documented in June 2024 record abusive treatment of trans detainees by railway police. The Madras High Court's judgment of 7 June 2021 in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police issued sweeping guidelines on protecting LGBTQIA+ persons, police sensitisation and a ban on conversion therapy, with directions to the National Medical Commission and education authorities. Bans on conversion therapy from that judgment and from the National Medical Commission in 2022 coexist with clandestine networks still operating.

Facilities and care access are largely set at state level. Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Maharashtra and Odisha run transgender welfare boards coordinating housing subsidies, free sex reassignment surgery in public hospitals and pensions, and several states provide targeted welfare, housing and healthcare benefits for hijras. Nationally, the Ayushman Bharat scheme was expanded in April 2024 to cover transition-related healthcare for all members of the transgender community. In August 2024 the Ministry of Finance clarified that LGBTQ people face no restrictions on opening joint bank accounts or naming partners as beneficiaries.

Intersex minors remain at risk: reports document a history of infanticide and a strong parental preference for assigning intersex infants male through non-consensual operations, and the Madras High Court ordered Tamil Nadu in April 2019 to ban sex-selective surgeries on intersex infants.
tangentialFactors:
Conservative organisations including the Vishva Hindu Parishad and the Bajrang Dal have labelled same-sex marriage a Western attack on Indian culture and have occasionally targeted Pride events, which have been held annually in dozens of cities since the first parade in Kolkata in 1999.

Public opinion is mixed and shifting. A 2025 Pew Research Center survey found 59% of respondents still call homosexuality morally unacceptable, a 2023 Gallup poll showed 53% support for same-sex marriage, and a 2021 Ipsos survey of urban internet users found 17% identifying as non-heterosexual or non-cisgender. Demographic studies report a high prevalence of verbal abuse and physical violence against sexual minorities. The 2011 census recorded roughly 480,000 people identifying as transgender, a figure far below the current estimate of two million.

Acceptance is notably higher among urban youth and students at top-tier universities such as the IITs, which host support groups like Indradhanu at IIT Delhi and Saathi at IIT Bombay. Colleges such as the American College in Madurai teach specialised curricula on genderqueer and intersex human rights using works by transgender activists A. Revathi and Kalki Subramaniam.

Political visibility includes Shabnam Mausi, the first transgender elected official in 1998, transgender mayors and judges, and Menaka Guruswamy, who in March 2026 became India's first openly LGBTQ+ member of the national Parliament.
localsOnly:
Resident-facing protections rest on constitutional and regulatory grounds: the University Grants Commission prohibits bullying and ragging aimed at students based on sexual orientation or gender identity in higher education, and the Allahabad High Court's 2021 extension of Article 15 bars employment discrimination on sexual orientation grounds.

Welfare delivery is organised through state transgender welfare boards in Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Maharashtra and Odisha, which coordinate housing subsidies, free sex reassignment surgery in public hospitals and pension schemes, alongside targeted welfare, housing and healthcare benefits for hijras in several other states. The Ayushman Bharat scheme's April 2024 expansion puts transition-related healthcare within reach of the whole transgender community, and the August 2024 Ministry of Finance clarification removes restrictions on joint bank accounts and partner beneficiary designations for LGBTQ people.

Community organisations operate nationwide, including GayBombay, Good as You in Bangalore and Sappho for Equality in Kolkata.
outOfScopeNotes:
How the March 2026 recognition scheme will be applied in practice at passport offices, airports and police stations is unresolved in the sources; no implementing rules or reported refusals under the amendment are documented here.

Whether the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita's omission of gender-identity-specific sexual offences has since been remedied by amendment or judicial reading is not sourced.

The United Kingdom policy note's finding that police abuse is not systemic sits alongside specific documented incidents of custody and checkpoint abuse; the sources do not reconcile the two assessments.

The 2011 census figure of roughly 480,000 transgender people and the current estimate of two million are drawn from different methods and periods, and no reconciled count exists in the inventory.
